title: How to make a selection in Photoshop on Mac: step by step for version 27.11
metaTitle: How to Make a Selection in Photoshop on Mac (2026 Guide)
description: Learn how to make a selection in Photoshop on Mac with Object Selection, Select and Mask and the Mac keys for add, subtract and deselect.
targetKeyword: how to make a selection in photoshop on mac
intro: To make a selection in Photoshop on Mac, choose a selection tool from the toolbar and click or drag over the part of the image you want. Hold Shift to add to the selection, Option to subtract from it, and press Command+D when you want to clear it.
tldr: Pick Object Selection from the toolbar, hover over the object, then click it.
Hold Shift to add, Option to subtract, and Shift with Option to keep only the overlap.
Refine edges in Select > Select and Mask, then clear the selection with Command+D.
Use Select > Inverse to flip a selection, and confirm its shortcut in your menu.
Photoshop 27.11 needs macOS 14.0 or later. Older builds may name menus differently.

blocks.text: A selection is an outline that protects everything outside it. Anything inside can be moved, recolored, filtered or masked. Most Photoshop work starts with one, whether you are removing a background, changing a jacket color or sharpening only a face. This guide starts with the fastest route on a Mac, Object Selection, then covers the controls that clean up the result.
Find the selection tools on your Mac

Photoshop keeps its selection tools in the toolbar on the left side of the window. A small triangle in the corner of an icon means more tools are hiding under it. Click and hold that icon, and a flyout menu opens with the rest of the group.

Object Selection sits in the same toolbar slot as Quick Selection. If it is missing, click and hold Quick Selection, then choose Object Selection from the list. An iDownloadBlog tutorial from May 2025 describes the same click and hold setup.

items: Object Selection: hover over an object and click it. Photoshop finds the edges for you.
Quick Selection: paint over an area with a round tip. Best for shapes with clear edges.
Marquee tools: drag a rectangle or ellipse. Hold Shift while dragging to draw a perfect square or circle.
Lasso tools: trace the outline by hand when a click will not find the edge.

blocks.text: Make your first selection with Object Selection

Object Selection works best on one subject with a clear edge. A product on a plain background is a good first test. Open the file with File > Open, then click the layer you want to work on in the Layers panel.

Choose Object Selection in the toolbar. Look at the options bar across the top of the window. Turn on Object Finder, Sample All Layers and Hard Edge. Object Finder lights up objects as you hover, so you can click the right one.

Move the pointer over the image. When the object you want shows a colored outline, click it. If the wrong thing lights up, move the pointer slightly until the correct object is highlighted. Photoshop then draws the selection around it.

If Object Finder is off, the tool works differently. You draw first. Drag a rough rectangle or lasso around the object, and Photoshop refines the shape from what sits inside your line. This fallback helps when the object sits in a busy photo.
Add, subtract and intersect with Mac keys

Most selections need a second pass. Hold Shift and drag over a missed area to add it. Hold Option and drag across a part you grabbed by accident to remove it. Hold Shift and Option together to keep only what both areas share.

rows: Replaces the current selection with the new one.
Adds the new area to the existing selection.
Removes the new area from the existing selection.
Keeps only the overlap between the old and new areas.
Opens the refine panel for the current selection.
blocks.caption: Selection modes on a Mac. Hold the key while you click or drag.

items: Shift: adds the new area to the current selection.
Option: subtracts the new area from the current selection.
Shift + Option: keeps only the overlap between the two areas.
Shift while dragging a Marquee tool: constrains it to a square or circle.
Command + D: deselects everything. Use it before you start a new subject.
Command + I: inverts the selection, according to one community guide. Confirm it in the Select menu.

blocks.text: Refine the edge with Select and Mask

Edges decide whether a cutout looks real. Hair, fur, glass and soft shadows need more than a single click. Choose Select > Select and Mask from the Mac menu bar. Photoshop opens the refine panel and shows the result on the canvas.

Inside Select and Mask, the edge controls set how wide and soft the boundary is. Work on one area at a time. Check the result against a plain light background and a dark one to spot halos. Click OK when the edge looks right.

blocks.title: Version note
blocks.text: Menu names can shift between Photoshop builds. This guide draws on 27.11 coverage and community reports, not a test of every build. If a name differs, check the Select menu first.
Clean up, deselect and invert

When you finish, clear the selection with Select > Deselect or Command+D. A leftover selection limits every later edit to the same shape. People often forget it and paint on the wrong pixels without noticing.

To select everything outside the object, use Select > Inverse. An Adobe Community Quick Tip from 2022 lists Command+I for this. iDownloadBlog gives a different key and calls its own wording unclear. Test it on a spare file, then trust the key shown in your menu.
When the selection comes out wrong

Most bad selections come from a few causes: the wrong layer, a busy background or a processing setting. Start with the layer. Sample All Layers tells Object Selection to read the visible layers, so the subject is not missed on a separate layer.

Apple silicon Macs add a few known problems. In an Adobe Community thread about an M1 Max, staff suggested running Photoshop in Rosetta emulation mode. One user said turning Rosetta off fixed it, but they needed Rosetta for a legacy plugin. Choose the option your plugins allow.
The thread covers Photoshop 23.1.1 to 23.3.2, so it is old. Its results may not match your build. Test the same image on your own setup before you change any setting.
Mistakes people make on a Mac

items: Working on the wrong layer. The selection applies to the layer you clicked, not the one you see.
Leaving a selection active. Later edits only touch the area inside it.
Skipping the edge. A hard cutout often shows a bright halo on a new background.
Mixing up the keys. Shift adds, Option subtracts, and Shift with Option keeps the overlap.
Refining too early. Get the broad shape right, then work on the edge.

blocks.text: Worked example: cut out a mug on a plain background

Say you have a photo of a white mug on a gray table. Open the file, select the photo layer, and choose Object Selection. Turn on Object Finder, Sample All Layers and Hard Edge. Hover over the mug until it lights up, then click.

Look at the handle. The gap between the handle and the body is often missed. Hold Option and drag over the gap to remove it, or hold Shift and drag over any missed part of the handle. Zoom in to check each pass.

Open Select > Select and Mask, soften the edge a little, and click OK. Then choose Layer > Layer Mask > Reveal Selection. The mug stays visible, the table is hidden, and the original photo stays intact for later edits.
Version and Mac requirements

The latest release at the time of writing is Photoshop 27.11, which CG Channel reported in October 2026. It requires macOS 14.0 or later, and Windows 10 or later. If your Mac runs an older system, check your version before you follow the menu names here.

Photoshop 27.11 adds Enhance Edge in the contextual task bar. It refines masks made by Remove Background. CG Channel says it is not a change to Select and Mask. To cut out a subject without its background, read [how to remove background in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/remove-a-background-in-photoshop).
What to do next

Practice on a few photos: a product on white, a person against a wall, and a plant against a sky. Each one teaches a different kind of edge. When your cutout needs a new frame, read [how to change canvas size in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/change-canvas-size-in-photoshop).

If you do this work every day, the [Photoshop page for designers](/for/designers/photoshop) collects workflows and shortcuts. Start with one object and one pass, and widen the job only when the first cutout looks right.

faq.question: Is Object Selection the best tool for every photo?
faq.answer: No. It works best on one clear subject with an edge Photoshop can read. For hair, fur or a busy background, paint rough areas with Quick Selection first, then refine in Select and Mask.

faq.question: Which key adds to a selection on a Mac?
faq.answer: Shift. Hold it while you click or drag. Option subtracts, and Shift with Option keeps only the overlap between the old and new areas.

faq.question: How do I deselect in Photoshop on a Mac?
faq.answer: Press Command+D or choose Select > Deselect. Do this before you start a new subject, so the next edit does not land inside the old outline.

faq.question: Why does my selection come out empty in Select and Mask?
faq.answer: Community reports describe this on older builds, including a Catalina thread about Photoshop CC 2020. Make a selection before you open Select and Mask, and check Adobe's current reset steps before you change preferences.

faq.question: Does the newest Photoshop change these steps?
faq.answer: Photoshop 27.11 adds Enhance Edge for Remove Background masks, and CG Channel says it is not a change to Select and Mask. Menu names can still differ between builds, so check the Select menu.

faq.question: Can Lazur make the selection for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur sees your screen while you hold the shortcut, points at the tool and explains each step out loud. It does not click buttons or work inside Photoshop for you.

task: Make a selection in Photoshop on Mac
appliesTo: Photoshop 27.11 and older on macOS 14.0 or later
requirements: Photoshop 27.11 or an older build on macOS 14.0 or later
A photo with one clear subject for the first try
The layer you want to change selected in the Layers panel

steps.name: Open your photo in Photoshop
steps.text: Choose File > Open, pick the image, and wait for it to appear on the canvas. Photoshop opens the file in its own document window. If the file is a PSD, check that its layers look right before you start.
steps.tip: Duplicate the layer first if you want to keep the original pixels untouched.

steps.name: Select the layer you want to change
steps.text: Click the layer in the Layers panel. Object Selection reads the layer you choose, so a click on the wrong layer picks the wrong object. Turn on Sample All Layers if the subject spans several layers.

steps.name: Find Object Selection in the toolbar
steps.text: Look at the toolbar on the left. If you see a Quick Selection icon, click and hold it. Pick Object Selection from the flyout. If it is missing, the toolbar may be hidden.
steps.tip: Long-press Quick Selection if Object Selection does not appear.

steps.name: Set the options bar
steps.text: Across the top of the window, turn on Object Finder, Sample All Layers and Hard Edge. Object Finder highlights objects as you hover. Hard Edge gives a crisp boundary, which suits products and shapes with clean lines.

steps.name: Hover and click the object
steps.text: Move the pointer over the subject. Wait for the object to light up with an outline, then click. If the highlight covers the wrong thing, move the pointer until the right object lights up.

steps.name: Draw a rough shape if Object Finder is off
steps.text: With Object Finder turned off, drag a rough rectangle or lasso around the object. Photoshop refines the shape from what is inside your line. Keep your rough line close to the edge but outside the subject.

steps.name: Add missing areas
steps.text: Hold Shift and click or drag over the part that was missed. Keep the key held until the area is inside the selection. Shift is the Add To key, so the new area joins the old one.

steps.name: Remove unwanted areas
steps.text: Hold Option and drag over the area to remove, such as a shadow or a nearby object. Hold Shift and Option together to keep only the overlap between the old and new areas.

steps.name: Open Select and Mask
steps.text: With the selection active, choose Select > Select and Mask. Photoshop opens the refine panel and shows the result on the canvas. Use it to soften or sharpen the edge, especially on hair and soft shadows.

steps.name: Confirm the edge, then deselect
steps.text: Click OK to return to the document. Clear the selection with Select > Deselect when you are done. The marching ants disappear, and edits apply to the whole layer again.

steps.name: Invert the selection if you need the rest
steps.text: To select everything outside the object, choose Select > Inverse. Command+I is listed for this in one community guide. Check the menu for the shortcut your build uses.
steps.tip: Test on a spare file first, because sources disagree on this key.

troubleshooting.problem: Toolbar tools do not respond on macOS Sonoma 14.1
troubleshooting.fix: One report on Photoshop 25.1.0 says tools vanished when clicked and the desktop showed through. A community workaround is to turn on Application Frame, float the toolbar, then turn Application Frame off. It lasts only until the toolbar docks again. One user said macOS 14.1.1 fixed it, while another saw it on macOS 14.7.2 with Photoshop 26.2.0. The fix is not confirmed.

In a Catalina thread on Photoshop CC 2020, a user said resetting all preferences fixed it. The thread gives no reset path, and a Windows user said reset did not help. Make a selection first, then open Select and Mask.

troubleshooting.problem: Object Selection highlights the wrong object
troubleshooting.fix: Turn on Object Finder and hover slowly until the right object lights up. If nothing works, turn Object Finder off and draw a rough rectangle around the subject.

troubleshooting.problem: Selection looks wrong on Apple silicon
troubleshooting.fix: Select Subject results varied on an M1 Max in a thread from Photoshop 23. Test the same image on your build first. Test Rosetta on and off only if your plugins allow it.
Open the Select menu and choose Inverse. Read the shortcut beside it. Sources disagree on the key, so the menu is the reliable check.
